message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
I believe this is one of the strongest applications we have put together. The need is documented, not asserted: our household numbers are up by around two-thirds in two years, and we can quantify exactly how much fresh food we are turning away, 1.2 tonnes a week, because we log every declined offer. The project responds directly to that gap and nothing more. The budget is lean: we got competing quotes for the cold room and the electrics and took the lower figure each time, and the van comes with a warranty. The value for money is exceptional, at roughly 33p per meal in the first year and falling to almost nothing over the equipment's ten-year life. We have thought about the long term too: this is a one-off capital investment with written supermarket commitments behind it, so it will keep delivering without coming back to funders. Our monitoring is concrete and measurable. I am confident the Foundation will see this as exactly the kind of lasting capacity-building its fund exists for.
</author>

<document>
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.
</document>
response:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank chilled storage application

The case for the project is real: rising demand, a quantified gap, a clear fix, and a tidy budget. But several problems would likely be spotted by an assessor, and one of them undermines the sustainability argument you're relying on most.

## Major issues

**1. Running costs vs. reserves, and the sustainability claim**
- Section 5 commits you to about **£11,000 a year** in new running costs (£4,200 electricity plus £6,800 van).
- Against that you show an unrestricted surplus of **£900** and unrestricted reserves of **£5,100**. On those figures, the reserves would be gone in about six months.
- Section 8 then says the equipment "will be sustainable without further grant funding." The application's own numbers contradict this, and an assessor reading sections 5 and 8 together will notice.
- Capital funds usually ask exactly this question: will the applicant be able to run what we buy? You need a credible plan for the £11,000. Options include confirmed or applied-for revenue funding, a supermarket or partner contribution to fuel and energy, savings on bought-in food as donated fresh food replaces purchases, or fundraising targets. Then rewrite section 8 to describe that plan rather than claiming no further funding is needed.

**2. The growth figure is wrong**
- 410 to 620 households is an increase of **51%**, not 66%. (620 is 151% of 410.)
- Your summary says "around two-thirds." It's closer to half. Correct it: an arithmetic error in the headline statistic damages credibility across the whole application.

**3. The timetable is already out of date**
- Section 7 says the equipment will be in service "by October 2026." That date has passed.
- Even ordering immediately on award, the eight-week installation lead time means early 2027 at the earliest. Give a realistic date, ideally relative to the award date.

**4. Three distribution sites or four?**
- Section 1 lists three sites (Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge, Over Hollins). Section 3 says the van will serve "our four distribution sites."
- Either fix the number, or explain the fourth site (e.g. if the warehouse also distributes).

## Significant weaknesses

**5. The cost-per-meal figure only counts the capital**
- 33p per meal (£48,600 ÷ 147,600) is arithmetically correct. But it leaves out the £11,000 running costs, which adds about 7.5p per meal every year.
- Including them, year one is about **40p per meal**.
- Your summary's claim that the cost falls "to almost nothing" over ten years isn't true once running costs are counted. It levels off at roughly 10–12p per meal. That is still very good value, so present it honestly; it's a strong number.

**6. The ten-year life doesn't fit the van**
- A three-year-old van with 40,000 miles and a 12-month warranty is unlikely to last ten more years of depot runs.
- Either give the van a realistic life (perhaps five to seven years) or explain your replacement plan. The cold room's ten-year life is more believable, and you could cite the supplier's figure.

**7. The strongest evidence is missing from the document**
- Your summary says you log every declined offer, which is exactly what makes the 1.2 tonne figure credible. The application doesn't say so.
- Add a sentence on how the figure was recorded and over what period. Offer the log as supporting evidence.
- Do the same for the supermarket letters: attach them, and say what they commit to (volumes, frequency, duration). "Continue to offer surplus" doesn't guarantee the tonnage the project depends on.

**8. The distribution logistics are unaddressed**
- Chilled surplus often has very short shelf life, and your sites open on different days.
- An assessor will ask whether 1.2 tonnes a week can actually reach families before use-by dates. They'll also ask whether the sites can keep food cold during sessions, given there's no equipment budget for them.
- They may also ask who drives the van and whether volunteers have food hygiene and temperature-control training.
- A short paragraph covering these points would close an obvious gap.

**9. Ambitious target**
- Moving fresh-produce parcels from under 10% to 80% within six months is a large jump. Explain why it's achievable, or set staged targets.
- Also give a baseline for the client feedback survey so there's something to measure progress against.

## Smaller points

- **Premises:** if the warehouse is leased, confirm landlord consent for the cold room and electrical work, and that the lease runs long enough to justify the investment.
- **Van quote:** you have only one quote for the van. Either get a second or explain why (e.g. limited availability of refrigerated vans).
- **Meals figure:** 62.4 t × 2,380 is about 148,500 meals. Rounding to 62 t first gives 147,600. This is trivial, but be consistent, and name the source of the 2,380 conversion factor (e.g. WRAP or FareShare).

## What works well

- The need is specific and quantified, and the project is closely matched to it.
- The budget adds up correctly (£48,600), is itemised, and is supported by competing quotes.
- The monitoring measures are concrete and directly linked to the outcome.
- The fit with a capacity-building capital fund is clear.

## Bottom line

Fix the four factual errors: the percentage, the date, the site count, and the "no further funding" claim. Above all, add a believable plan for the £11,000 annual running costs. With those changes, this could be a strong application. As it stands, the gap between section 5 and section 8 is the most likely reason it would be turned down.
